title: Nernst equation
examples: How do I use the Nernst equation if the concentrations are not one?
What does 'non-standard conditions' mean for the cell potential calculation?
Can I use the Nernst equation for a reaction that isn't in an acidic solution?

explain.say: Today we look at the Nernst equation for cell potential.
The standard cell potential uses standard conditions always.
When concentrations change, we use the Nernst equation.
The reaction quotient Q uses current concentrations values.
For standard temperature, we often simplify the equation greatly.
In a real battery, the concentration of ions changes over time.

draw.text: Battery voltage drops as ions are used.

faq.q: Do I always have to use the natural logarithm in the Nernst equation?
faq.a: No, if the problem specifies standard temperature and uses base ten logarithms, you can use the simplified form.
asks: Should I use ln or log?
What base of logarithm should I use?

faq.q: What happens to the potential if the product concentration increases?
faq.a: If product concentrations increase, the reaction quotient Q increases, making the potential E lower.
asks: Does high product concentration lower voltage?
How does Q affect the potential?

faq.q: Does the temperature affect the calculation significantly?
faq.a: Yes, temperature changes affect the value of the gas constant R and the overall potential calculation.
asks: How does temperature change the equation?

faq.q: If the reaction is reversible, can I use the Nernst equation?
faq.a: Yes, the Nernst equation applies to any reversible electrochemical cell reaction.
asks: Can I use this for non-spontaneous reactions?

faq.q: Is Q the same as the equilibrium constant K?
faq.a: No, Q uses current concentrations, while K is the constant value at equilibrium.
asks: What is the difference between Q and K?
When do I use K instead of Q?

facts: The Nernst equation calculates cell potential under non-standard conditions.
The reaction quotient Q is calculated using the current concentrations of species.
At standard conditions, the potential E equals E degrees.
The equation simplifies when using base ten logarithms at twenty-nine degrees Celsius.

quiz.say: A cell has a standard potential of one point one volt. If the product concentration increases, the new potential will be:
quiz.show: Potential decreases as product concentration rises.

options.show: Higher than one point one volt
options.say: Higher than one point one volt

options.show: Exactly the same as one point one volt
options.say: Exactly the same as one point one volt

options.show: Lower than one point one volt
options.say: Lower than one point one volt

quiz.why: Increasing product concentration increases Q, which makes the term (RT/nF)ln(Q) larger, thus lowering E.

wrong.0: This incorrectly suggests that higher product concentration drives the reaction forward more strongly.
wrong.1: This ignores the effect of non-standard concentrations on the cell potential.
wrong.2: This suggests the reaction stops completely, which is only true at equilibrium.

quiz.say: If the concentration of reactants decreases, the cell potential will:
quiz.show: Potential increases when reactant concentration drops.
quiz.why: Decreasing reactant concentration lowers Q, making the term (RT/nF)ln(Q) smaller, thus increasing E.

wrong.1: This suggests that lower reactant concentration makes the reaction less favorable.
wrong.2: This incorrectly assumes that concentration changes have no effect on the cell potential.
wrong.3: This is too extreme; the potential changes, but not necessarily to a negative value.

quiz.say: If the temperature increases, the Nernst equation predicts that the cell potential will:
quiz.show: Higher temperature changes the potential value.

options.show: Change according to the temperature term
options.say: Change according to the temperature term

quiz.why: The temperature T is a variable in the equation, so changing it changes the calculated potential.

wrong.0: Temperature is explicitly included in the equation as T, so it must affect the result.
wrong.2: The change depends on the specific reaction and the value of the constant R.
wrong.3: This assumes a linear relationship that is not guaranteed by the equation.
